title: Synchronization: One at a Time, Please!
concept: When multiple threads access a shared resource (like a single-stall restroom) at the same time, accidents happen. That's when you need a 'lock (synchronized)'.

steps.title: main Method Starts
steps.explanation:
**`public static void main(String[] args)`**

The program's entry point.
We create a bank account and begin the mission.

steps.title: Creating the Account Object
steps.explanation:
A `BankAccount` object is created to serve as the shared resource.
This object internally holds an invisible 'monitor lock (key)'.

steps.title: Synchronized Method
steps.explanation:
When `synchronized` is placed before a method, any thread that wants to execute this method must first acquire the key (lock) of that object (`account`).
Only one thread at a time can execute this method.

steps.title: Critical Section
steps.explanation:
Only the thread holding the key can safely modify `balance`.
Other threads must wait outside until this operation completes.
A code region where only one thread can execute at a time is called a 'Critical Section'.

quiz.question: How many locks can a Java object have?
options: As many as the number of threads
quiz.explanation:
Every Java object has exactly one 'monitor lock'.
That's why only one thread at a time can enter a synchronized region.

misconceptions.wrong: Using more synchronized makes the program faster.
misconceptions.correct: No! Synchronization forces threads to line up, which actually degrades performance.
misconceptions.why:
Waiting time is introduced.
Use it minimally and only on shared resources that truly need protection.

keyTakeaway: synchronized is a 'shield that protects data from corruption'. Remember: there's only one key per object!
